results.title: Sample size considerations for stratified cluster randomization design with binary outcomes and varying cluster size
results.content: We propose closed-form sample size formulas for estimating the required total number of subjects and for estimating the number of clusters for each group per stratum, based on Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel statistic for stratified cluster randomization design with binary outcomes, accounting for both clustering and varying cluster size. In this paper, we propose closed-form sample size formulas for estimating the required total number of subjects and for estimating the number of clusters for each group per stratum, for stratified CRTs with binary outcomes and varying cluster size. In Section 2, we present notations and the method for sample size estimations for the required total number of subjects and for the number of clusters for each group per stratum based on Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel statistic, adjusting for both clustering and varying cluster size. Then, the sample size can be obtained by solving the following two equations: Based on Equations (1) and (2), the total number of subjects _N_ required for stratified cluster randomization design is given by The estimated total number of subjects _N_ depends on the mean and variance of the distribution of cluster size, in addition to the expected group difference, ICC, and type _I_ and type _II_ error. We conduct simulation studies to assess the performance of the proposed sample size approach for estimating the required number of clusters for each group per stratum for stratified CRTs with varying cluster size, under various design configurations. This suggests that the proposed method derived based on the large sample theory is widely applicable to stratified CRTs with varying cluster size and maintains the desired power in scenarios where the number of clusters per group per stratum is relatively small. results.title: Survey Sample Size Optimization Techniques
results.content: Our exploration covers the design effect and its mathematical underpinnings, the rationale and mechanics behind data weighting, necessary adjustments when dealing with cluster sampling, and techniques designed to mitigate bias. * **Post-Stratification Weights:** After data collection, researchers might adjust the weights so that the survey sample better reflects known population totals, such as age, gender, or education level. Several software solutions offer integrated routines for survey sample size optimization, design effect adjustments, weighting, and bias mitigation. From the fundamentals of the design effect and the calculation of effective sample sizes to advanced weighting adjustments, cluster corrections, and bias mitigation strategies, every element plays a critical role in ensuring that survey results are robust and accurate. Through this article, we have seen how design effect modification can necessitate sample size adjustments, the role of weighting in correcting sample imbalances, the intricacies introduced by clustering, and the multiple strategies available to mitigate bias.
